question.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 14 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
question.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set ${v,w}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{4\cdot 3+14\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (-1)}{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}v=3[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{4\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (-2)}{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}w=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10 \\ -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Map Relative to Two Bases Given One Basis
question.problem:
Consider the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ of the vector space $V$ and the basis $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ given by

$$
C={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Find the matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the map $T:V\to {R}^{2}$ relative to these bases if 

$$
T({b}_{1})=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,T({b}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that $[T]_{B|C}$ is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $C.$

First, we need to find the coordinates of $T({b}_{i})$ relative to the basis $C$ for each $i=1,2.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the following matrix:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 & -4 \\ 4 & 6 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 4 & 6 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the right-hand side gives the matrix of the linear transformation relative to the bases $B$ and $C:$

$$
[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -8 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis Using a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
question.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
question.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-1\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 3 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -36 \\ 14 & -25\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Components of a Vector Orthogonal to a Set
question.problem: Given that $u=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]$ is a non-zero  vector that is orthogonal to the set $W={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]},$ find the value of $\frac{b+c}{a}.$
question.worked_solution:
The vector $u$ is orthogonal to the set $W$ if $u\cdot {w}_{1}=0$ and $u\cdot {w}_{2}=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}u\cdot {w}_{1}=0 \\ u\cdot {w}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+7{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -5 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ⇔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & \frac{7}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & \frac{7}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{5}{2} & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd), so ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{3}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{5}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=6,$ we get the vector 
$[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 15 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, we obtain $a=1,$ $b=15,$ and $c=6.$

Finally, $\frac{b+c}{a}=\frac{15+6}{1}=21.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
question.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 15 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 15 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & -5 \\ -5 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -9\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & -9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & -7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+7{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 1 & 11\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{54}[\begin{aligned}11 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 1 & 11\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{54}[\begin{aligned}11 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to the Standard Basis
question.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
question.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/db/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -8 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 10 \\ -6 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Multiple Parts of the Decomposition
question.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i}-7 \\ 4\text{i}+3\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7+4\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i}-7 \\ 4\text{i}+3\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Using the Complex Conjugate
question.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i}-1 \\ \text{i}+2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2+3\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=2-3\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}-1-2\text{i} \\ 2-\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Cross Product Using Determinants
question.problem: Let $u=⟨-3,10,4⟩$ and $v=⟨4,7,1⟩.$ Find $u\times v.$
question.worked_solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u\times v & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3 & 10 & 4 \\ 4 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-3 & 10 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(10\cdot 1-4\cdot 7)i-((-3)\cdot 1-4\cdot 4)j+((-3)\cdot 7-10\cdot 4)k \\  & =(10-28)i-(-3-16)j+(-21-40)k \\  & =-18i+19j-61k \\  & =⟨-18,19,-61⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded By a Curve When It Crosses the X-Axis Several Times
question.problem:
![](images/8b/8b7b81c97a842b82c2e4cbbd041883c1bd7f4f4ab58dc6592c12ec1cc0262620.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-2x-3) & =0 \\ x(x+1)(x-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=-1,x=0$ or $x=3.$ Since $0\in [-1,3],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we have

$$
{A}_{1}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that for $x\in [0,3]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{2}=-{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}-({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}-({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Constructing an Integral That Gives the Area Bounded by a Curve
question.problem:
![](images/8b/8b729d243b344df6b26757773bf0521dea80da34fc727541d24babd3732563cf.png)

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is given by the integral expression below. What is the value of $a?$

$$
A={\int }_{-1}^{a}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x-{\int }_{a}^{5/2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x.
$$
question.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4} & =0 \\ -\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4} & =-4 \\ {x}^{4} & =16 \\ \sqrt[4]{{x}^{4}} & =\pm \sqrt[4]{16} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt[4]{{2}^{4}} \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=-1$ and $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is $x=2.$

Since $2\in [-1,\frac{5}{2}],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=2$ to $x=\frac{5}{2}.$

So, $a=2$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{-1}^{2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{5/2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x.
$$

$$

Since $2\in [-1,\frac{5}{2}],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=2$ to $x=\frac{5}{2}.$

So, $a=2$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{-1}^{2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{5/2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x.

question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 8 & 5\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}11 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

where ${v}_{i}$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $V.$

question.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Distinct Eigenvalues
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the QR Factorization of a Matrix
question.problem:
$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{31}\cdot {r}_{12}.$
question.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-(\frac{4}{2})[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{31}\cdot {r}_{12}=(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=-2.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System
question.problem:
Find the least-squares solution to the system of linear equations given below. You're given that the columns of the corresponding coefficient matrix are linearly independent.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=1 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=7 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-4\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 7 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}}\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 7 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 28 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{84}[\begin{aligned}21 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 28 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Columns of the First Matrix Given Part of an SVD With a Zero Eigenvalue
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -6 & 8\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and ${\sigma }_{i}\ne 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

$$
{u}_{i}=\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{i}}A{v}_{i},
$$

 

where ${u}_{i}$ and ${v}_{i}$ are the $i$th columns of the orthogonal matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively.  

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -6 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Third Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}14 & 10 \\ 10 & 14\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=24,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-24I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -10 \\ 10 & 14\end{aligned}]-24[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-10 & 10 \\ 10 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-24I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & 10 \\ 10 & 14\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}10 & 10 \\ 10 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-4I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix
question.problem:
A study conducted on $3\,400$ teenagers by the transportation department of a particular city reveals that teenagers' preference for the type of home-to-school transportation changes with time. The following table shows the results of this study.  

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Bus** | **Bicycle** | **Electric Scooter ** |
| To: | **Bus** | $0.2$ | $0.2$ | $0$ |
| **Bicycle** | $0.4$ | $0.4$ | $0.4$ |  |
| **Electric Scooter** | $0.4$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ |  |

For example, $40%$ of teenagers who used to go to school by bus now go by bicycle.  

How many teenagers would eventually go to school on electric scooters if the listed probabilities remained constant over many years?
question.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=5{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{5}{2}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+(\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3})-{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{4}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 2{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{4}{10} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{1}{2}$ of the teenagers will go to school in electric scooters. Therefore, the total number of teenagers in the city that will go to school in electric scooters will be

$$
\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\,400=1\,700.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Recognizing Parts of the Invertible Matrix Theorem
question.problem:
$T$ is a bijection $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{n} \\  & =n \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 
$\,⟺\,$  $T$ is invertible

Consider the equivalence above, where $T:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following should be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the *invertible matrix theorem* (in terms of linear transformations) states the following: 

 $T$ is a bijection $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=n \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 
$\,⟺\,$  $T$ is invertible

Therefore, the missing expression is $\text{rank}(T).$

question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector as a Sum or Difference of More Than Two Known Vectors
question.problem:
![](images/0c/0c681289ee631de241f876091878b84cd9497c5d8e71d27512f9a832c242329b.png)

Consider the diagram shown above, where $\overset{\to }{QP}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{RS}=b,$ $\overset{\to }{RT}=c,$ and $\overset{\to }{RP}=d.$ Find $\overset{\to }{QS}$ in terms of $a,b,c,$ and $d.$
question.worked_solution:
We want to find a "path" from $Q$ to $S$ consisting only of the vectors $a,b,c,$ and $d.$ 

According to the triangle law of addition,

$$
\overset{\to }{QS}=\overset{\to }{QP}+\overset{\to }{PR}+\overset{\to }{RS}
$$

as shown below.

![](images/31/317d78cec35bc3721ebbd64ac1ed53aa5b36c89101a170b93805d17c670f2673.png)

  

Now, from the original diagram, we have that

$$
\overset{\to }{QP}=a,\,\overset{\to }{PR}=-d,\,\overset{\to }{RT}=b.
$$

Let's add these to our diagram.

![](images/ff/ff4b4292bb8a15551cb22da1f621684e9fdf24d35ae873b408dc612e5b3255e8.png)

   

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{QS} & =\overset{\to }{QP}+\overset{\to }{PR}+\overset{\to }{RS} \\  & =a-d+b.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation Given a Corresponding Perfect Square
question.problem:
Solve the equation $4{x}^{2}+24x=-11.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}+6x+9$ is a perfect square.*
question.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+24x & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+6x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-{3}^{2}] & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-9] & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $36$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36+36 & =-11+36 \\ 4(x+3)^{2} & =25 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |x+3| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ x+3 & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-3\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{11}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Graph of a Strict Inequality Given in Standard Form
question.problem: Which of the following shaded areas describes the region bounded by the inequality $4x-2y<6?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we convert the inequality into slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-2y & <6 \\ -2y & <-4x+6 \\ 2y & >4x-6 \\ y & >2x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed as usual. We start by drawing the corresponding straight line 

$$
y=2x-3.
$$

 Since the inequality involves a 'strictly greater than' sign, the line $y=2x-3$ itself is *not* part of the solution. Therefore, we draw a **dashed line**.

Then, we need to decide whether to shade above or below the line. The inequality 

$$
y>2x-3
$$

 refers to the $y$-values that are *greater than* those on the line $y=2x-3,$ so we shade *above* the line.

![](images/2f/2fe69dace2487c1b6dc73fcd122fd358513d8ac9528b3195d2075f8b62c75b4a.png)

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Graph of a Non-Strict Inequality Given in Standard Form
question.problem: Which of the following shaded areas describes the region bounded by the inequality $x+2y\le 4?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we convert the inequality into slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & \le 4 \\ 2y & \le -x+4 \\ y & \le -\frac{1}{2}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed as usual. We start by drawing the corresponding straight line 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2.
$$

 Since the inequality involves a 'less than *or equal to*' sign, the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2$ itself is part of the solution. Therefore, we draw a **solid line**. 

Then, we need to decide whether to shade above or below the line. The inequality 

$$
y\le -\frac{1}{2}x+2
$$

 refers to the $y$-values that are *less than* or equal to those on the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2,$ so we shade *below* the line. 

![](images/8b/8b906cf167528f484109528a93732dc2b8d73558bb02f454bb520af87efde3c5.png)

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Rank or Nullity of a Matrix Given a Description of the Column or Null Space
question.problem: Let $A$ be a $4\times 5$ matrix. If $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(A)$, find $\text{dim(Null}(A)).$
question.worked_solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector as a Sum or Difference of More Than Two Known Vectors
question.problem:
![](images/a8/a89c73fd1e50e3c2d28694a366c79c75ad5f1bbf63a5c1333a7d7b62f5a4a0e9.png)

Consider the diagram shown above, where $\overset{\to }{QP}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{RQ}=b,$ $\overset{\to }{SQ}=c,$ and $\overset{\to }{RT}=d.$ Find $\overset{\to }{TP}$ in terms of $a,b,c,$ and $d.$
question.worked_solution:
We want to find a "path" from $T$ to $P$ consisting only of the vectors $a,b,c,$ and $d.$ 

According to the triangle law of addition,

$$
\overset{\to }{TP}=\overset{\to }{TR}+\overset{\to }{RQ}+\overset{\to }{QP}
$$

 

as shown below.

![](images/e0/e0e6351dfbef6dadf6a6fb179f1545622ddaeab24c2c06dee03c87821304695c.png)

 

Now, from the original diagram, we have that

$$
\overset{\to }{TR}=-d,\,\overset{\to }{RQ}=b,\,\overset{\to }{QP}=a.
$$

Let's add these to our diagram. 

![](images/02/02899ac9c536b0020514780db617e29977a5dc4daf60f42d80ed671883327fe3.png)

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{TP} & =\overset{\to }{TR}+\overset{\to }{RQ}+\overset{\to }{QP} \\  & =-d+b+a \\  & =a+b-d.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Graph of a Non-Strict Inequality Given in Standard Form
question.problem: Which of the following shaded areas describes the region bounded by the inequality $3x-2y\ge 6?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we convert the inequality into slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2y & \ge 6 \\ -2y & \ge -3x+6 \\ y & \le \frac{3}{2}x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed as usual. We start by drawing the corresponding straight line 

$$
y=\frac{3}{2}x-3.
$$

 Since the inequality involves a 'less than *or equal to*' sign, the line $y=\frac{3}{2}x-3$ itself is part of the solution. Therefore, we draw a **solid line**.

Then, we need to decide whether to shade above or below the line. The inequality 

$$
y\le \frac{3}{2}x-3
$$

 refers to the $y$-values that are *less than* or equal to those on the line $y=\frac{3}{2}x-3,$ so we shade *below* the line.

![](images/ea/ea12ed8d62304ecdc90859d5cd206045cef852522ce16c67a9307ddbd755b3dc.png)

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following is the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
To find the image of the triangle under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of the triangle:

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are $(-9,3)$, $(-9,3),$ $(3,-1).$ Notice that all three points lie on the same line.

So, the image of our triangle under the action of $T$ is as follows:

question.knowledge_point: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-2y)\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=2-\frac{x}{2}$ for $\,0\le x\le 2?$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=2-\frac{t}{2}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,2-\frac{t}{2}⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\frac{t}{2})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-2y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}-2(2-\frac{t}{2})={t}^{3}+t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({t}^{3}+t-4)\cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}({t}^{3}+t-4)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating an Outward-Pointing Unit Normal Vector for a Positively Oriented Curve
question.problem: The closed curve $C$ is defined as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=7.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
question.worked_solution:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{7},
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2}$ on $[0,3]?$
question.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{9}(\frac{3}{2})6{x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{1/2}={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}(2{x}^{3}+1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given a QR Factorization
question.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & 24 \\ -24 & -7\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -24 \\ 24 & -7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-(2) & =-11 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
question.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}11 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}11 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
question.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Sketching the Domain of a Multivariable Function
question.problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the function $g(x,y)=\frac{y}{2-x}?$
question.worked_solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following condition is satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequality:

$$
2-x\ne 0\,⟹\,x\ne 2
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
question.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution to a Weighted Least-Squares Problem
question.problem:
Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & 9 \\ 9 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & ={[\begin{aligned}14 & 9 \\ 9 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{14\cdot 9-9\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}9 & -9 \\ -9 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{45}[\begin{aligned}45 \\ -45\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Vector Given Its Image Under a Linear Transformation
question.problem:
The vector $v$ in the plane is mapped to the vector $[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ under the action of the linear transformation $T$ whose matrix $T$ is given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the original vector $v?$
question.worked_solution:
From the given information, we have 

$$
T\cdot v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

We need to reverse the action of the matrix $T.$ So, we multiply the above equation by ${T}^{-1},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}\cdot T\cdot v & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ v & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to calculate the inverse of $T$, which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-6-(-4)}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the original vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Image of a Square
question.problem:
![](images/5f/5f91cc8b30f9b764021cd84c374a328c7ffb1287a9f0dc6a211a3fadfac2fdbd.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1}
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=v,\,y=u(1+{v}^{2}).
$$

Find the image of $Δ$ under the action of $T.$ 

*Hint: You may assume that $T$ has no critical points in the interior of $Δ.$*
question.worked_solution:
We're told that $T$ has no critical points in the interior of $Δ.$ So, to map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $Δ$ separately:

- Consider the image of the side ${S}_{1},$ where we have $v=0$ and $0\le u\le 1.$ Substituting $v=0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) &  \\  & =(v,\,u(1+{v}^{2})) &  \\  & =(0,\,u(1+{0}^{2})) &  \\  & =(0,\,u), & 0\le u\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a vertical line segment traversed from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(0,1)$ in the $xy$-plane.

- Consider the image of the side ${S}_{2}.$ Here, we have $u=1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$ Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) &  \\  & =(v,\,u(1+{v}^{2})) &  \\  & =(v,\,1(1+{v}^{2})) &  \\  & =(v,\,1+{v}^{2}), & 0\le v\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an upward-opening parabola traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,2)$ in the $xy$-plane.

- Consider the image of the side ${S}_{3}.$ Here, we have $v=1$ and $1\ge u\ge 0.$ Substituting $v=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) &  \\  & =(v,\,u(1+{v}^{2})) &  \\  & =(1,\,u(1+{1}^{2})) &  \\  & =(1,\,2u), & 1\ge u\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a vertical line segment traversed from the point $(1,2)$ to the point $(1,0)$ in the $xy$-plane.

- Consider the image of the side ${S}_{4}.$ Here, we have $u=0$ and $1\ge v\ge 0.$ Substituting $u=0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) &  \\  & =(v,\,u(1+{v}^{2})) &  \\  & =(v,\,0(1+{v}^{2})) &  \\  & =(v,\,0), & 1\ge v\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
This is a horizontal line segment traversed from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane.

Drawing the images of the sides of our square, we obtain the following image of $Δ:$

![](images/46/468a2bf9e981f18b656fe1b5a023f98d1f5c990880caf5f9908c05cc3fe2d197.png)

question.knowledge_point: Finding Regions Where a Transformation is Orientation-Preserving or Reversing
question.problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-preserving?
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ 4u-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 \\ 4 & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv+4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4uv+4 & >0 \\ -4uv & >-4 \\ uv & <1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives the solution $v<\frac{1}{u}$ for $u>0$ and $v>\frac{1}{u}$ for $u<0.$

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=\frac{1}{u}
$$

defines a hyperbola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving must be the following:

![](images/fe/fe7bb422a3f992ea88a900e63b2c55df99bce3a785929901c248abadfadf23f1.png)

$$

$$

So, the matrix represents a rotation of $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians counterclockwise about the origin.

$$

$$

$$

question.worked_solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $Δ$ separately:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $\sqrt{2}\le u\le 2.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{\pi }{5}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{\pi }{5}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $2$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\frac{2\pi }{5}$ and $\sqrt{2}\le u\le 2.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{2\pi }{5}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{5}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{5})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{2\pi }{5}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $2$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=\sqrt{2}$ and $\frac{\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{2\pi }{5}.$ 

Substituting $u=\sqrt{2}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{5}.$

- Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=2$ and $\frac{\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{2\pi }{5}.$ 

Substituting $u=2$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$

$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{5}.$

Therefore, the image $D$ of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=\sqrt{2}$ and $r=2,$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta =\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{5},$

$$

question.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $x={y}^{3}+1$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [0,1].$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that $x={y}^{3}+1\ge 0$ for all $y\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)={y}^{3}+1,$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(y)={y}^{3}+1,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(y)=3{y}^{2}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}+1)\sqrt{1+(3{y}^{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}+1)\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Converting an Integral Over a Region Enclosed Between Two Curves to Polar Coordinates
question.problem:
![](images/6d/6ddc0b2138025b07ffdb7bf34afabeba578400b194922bec7a733cc9246c7c0f.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2$ and the line $y=2-x,$ as shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
question.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at $(1,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =2 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =2 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2 & =2 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ r(r-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$

- For $y=2-x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2-x \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ r & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(2,0)$ and $(0,2).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/58/587c299c1bdf89061be205cf185d6335fba865d2e30c81cac5b9d223fc84b486.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\le r\le 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2/(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{2/(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =2 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =2 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2 & =2 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ r(r-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$

- For $y=2-x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2-x \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ r & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(2,0)$ and $(0,2).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14065827/assets/587c299c1bdf89061be205cf185d6335fba865d2e30c81cac5b9d223fc84b486.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\le r\le 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2/(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{2/(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Rectangular Preimage Given Its Image Under a Polar Transformation
question.problem:
![](images/22/22ed424a27d1674bc7f4316b0b644e3dbac4c9f460e23ea2aa6ee90cb74b4c5b.png)

Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, shown above. The transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),\,y(u,v)),
$$

where

$$
x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,
$$

maps the region $Δ$ from the $uv$-plane to $D.$ Which of the following could be the region $Δ?$
question.worked_solution:
For our transformation $T,$ we have

$$
x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v.
$$

Notice that if we change $u$ to $r$ and $v$ to $\theta ,$ we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

which represents the usual formulas for changing from polar to Cartesian coordinates. 

Therefore, the pre-image $Δ$ of $D$ under the action of $T$ is the region that can be written as 

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{3}\le v\le \frac{2\pi }{3}}.
$$

This is the rectangular region enclosed between

- two vertical lines with Cartesian equations $u=1$ and $u=\sqrt{3},$ and

- two horizontal lines with Cartesian equations $v=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $v=\frac{2\pi }{3},$

as shown in the diagram below.

question.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains
question.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=x{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y={x}^{2},$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=x{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/14/1419b067fe92945249655c5d29498aa4d3b0269d79ebd237fd9ed2a713b70b6a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})={y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})=2xy,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({y}^{2})}^{2}+(2xy)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Writing a Triple Integral as a Repeated Integral
question.problem:
Express the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+xy+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the box

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le 4,\,0\le z\le 5}
$$

as a repeated integral of the form 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{e}^{f}…\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Given the limits for $x,y,$ and $z,$ we can express our triple integral as a repeated integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+xy+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}+xy+{z}^{2}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$
