question.knowledge_point: Finding the Acceleration of a Particle Moving With Circular Motion
question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along a counterclockwise circular path centered at $O$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity of $2\,\text{rad/s}.$ Given that the particle is located at $(3,0)$ when $t=0,$ find the acceleration of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ seconds.
question.worked_solution:
The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius $a$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity $\omega $ is given by

$$
r(t)=a(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j),
$$

where it is assumed that the circle is centered at $O,$ and the particle is at the position $(a,0)$ when $t=0.$

In our case, we have $a=3$ and $\omega =2\text{ rad/s},$ so we get that the position function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

We find the velocity and acceleration vectors by differentiating. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j))^{′} \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j \\ a(t) & =(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the acceleration vector at $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})\,i-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})\,j \\  & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\,i-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\,j \\  & =-\frac{12}{2}\,i-\frac{12\sqrt{3}}{2}\,j \\  & =-6\,i-6\sqrt{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Image of a Vector Given With Respect to the Standard Basis Under a Linear Map
question.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 3 & 8 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ (shown above) and a basis $C$ of ${R}^{3}.$
The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to these bases, and the vector $x\in {R}^{2},$ are also given. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$
question.worked_solution:
We can find the coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $[x]_{B},$ the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B.$ So, let

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}].
$$

This gives us the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=3 \\ 3{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

We now row-reduce the corresponding augmented matrix using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 7 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 7 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -11 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 3 & 8 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}23 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}23 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -13 \\ 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity and Speed of a Particle Moving With Circular Motion
question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along a counterclockwise circular path centered at $O$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity of $2\,\text{rad/s}.$ Given that the particle is located at $(4,0)$ when $t=0,$ find the velocity of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$ seconds.
question.worked_solution:
The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius $R$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity $\omega $ is given by

$$
r(t)=R(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j),
$$

where it is assumed that the circle is centered at $O,$ and the particle is at the position $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$

In our case, we have $R=4$ and $\omega =2\text{ rad/s},$ so we get that the position function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

We find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =(4(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j))^{′} \\  & =-8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the velocity vector at $t=\frac{\pi }{8},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})\,i+8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})\,j \\  & =-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =-\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}\,i+4\sqrt{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Acceleration of a Particle Moving With Circular Motion
question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along a counterclockwise circular path centered at $O$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity of $4\,\text{rad/s}.$ Given that the particle is located at $(5,0)$ when $t=0,$ find the acceleration of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ seconds.
question.worked_solution:
The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius $a$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity $\omega $ is given by

$$
r(t)=a(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j),
$$

where it is assumed that the circle is centered at $O,$ and the particle is at the position $(a,0)$ when $t=0.$

In our case, we have $a=5$ and $\omega =4\text{ rad/s},$ so we get that the position function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

We find the velocity and acceleration vectors by differentiating. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =(5(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j))^{′} \\  & =-20\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,i+20\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j \\ a(t) & =(-20\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,i+20\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-80\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i-80\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the acceleration vector at $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-80\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,i-80\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,j \\  & =-80\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\,i-80\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )\,j \\  & =-80\,i\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Components of Acceleration at a Particular Moment
question.problem: The position $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t⟩,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds. Find the tangential component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=\pi \,\text{s}.$
question.worked_solution:
The tangential component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{T}=\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||}.
$$

First, we compute the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector and evaluating it at $t=\pi ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,1⟩, \\ v(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector and it evaluating at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩, \\ a(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $v(\pi )\cdot a(\pi )$ and $||v(\pi )||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\pi )\cdot a(\pi ) & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =0, \\ ||v(\pi )|| & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the tangential component of the acceleration at $t=\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{T} & =\frac{v(\pi )\cdot a(\pi )}{||v(\pi )||} \\  & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangential component of the acceleration is $0\,{\text{ms}}^{-2}.$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying Phase Lines From Graphs
question.problem:
![](images/1b/1bc88bc79f6cec9d8f2a9e44d397fda9d0a9a2cbe0691d542f25e2bdfa259dc1.png)

Consider the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ where the graph of $f(y)$ is shown above. Which of the following is the phase line corresponding to this differential equation?
question.worked_solution:
From the graph of the function $f(y),$ we can deduce the following information:

- The solutions to $f(y)=0$ are $y=-2,y=0$ and $y=2.$ Therefore $y=-2,0,2$ are the equilibrium solutions of the differential equation.

- $f(y)>0$ when $y\in (-\infty ,-2)\cup (0,2).$

- $f(y)<0$ when $y\in (-2,0)\cup (2,\infty ).$

Therefore, we can draw the phase line using the following recipe:

- Draw a vertical $y$-axis

- Mark the equilibrium solutions

- Draw arrows pointing up in the intervals where $f(y)>0$

- Draw arrows pointing down in the intervals where $f(y)<0$

Applying the above recipe, we get the following phase line for our differential equation.

![](images/66/66b90a2d1509ddb46e27d3e7164dbe1ab9b1f42aefd5df4b4482d8d2046f9bba.png)

question.knowledge_point: Reversing the Limits of Integration
question.problem:
Calculate 
${\int }_{0}^{1}2f(t)\,\text{d}t$
given that
${\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t=⟨1,\,-3,\,2⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨1,\,-3,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the scalar multiplication rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}2f(t)\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot ⟨-1,\,3,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,6,\,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Line That Corresponds to a Differential Equation
question.problem: Which of the following is the phase line of the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{2}-12y-35?$
question.worked_solution:
To draw the phase line of the differential equation, we proceed using the following three steps:

**Step 1**: Find the equilibrium solutions of the differential equation. 

In this case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{y}^{2}-12y-35 & =0 \\ -({y}^{2}+12y+35) & =0 \\ -(y+7)(y+5) & =0 \\ y & =-7,-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium solutions are $y=-7$ and $y=-5.$

**Step 2**: Find the intervals of $y$ for which $f(y)>0$ and $f(y)<0.$ 

Constructing a sign table, we get the following:

|  | $(-\infty ,-7)$ | $(-7,-5)$ | $(-5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-(y+7)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $y+5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-7,-5),$ and negative for $y\in (-\infty ,-7)\cup (-5,\infty ).$

**Step 3**: Draw the phase line using the following recipe:

- Draw a vertical $y$-axis

- Mark the equilibrium solutions

- Draw arrows pointing up in the intervals where $f(y)>0$

- Draw arrows pointing down in the intervals where $f(y)<0$

Applying the above recipe, we get the following phase line for our differential equation.

![](images/b0/b08c48590fe2538666e0e3a559c123b0f5cd3bb35680f2c98d3c14691780a575.png)

| $y-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-2,0)\cup (2,\infty ),$ and negative for $y\in (-\infty ,-2)\cup (0,2).$

question.problem:
A particular autonomous differential equation has the following properties:

- $y=-4$ and  $y=-1$ are equilibrium points

- $y=-1$ is a source

- $y=-4$ is a sink

Which of the following could be the phase line of the differential equation?
question.worked_solution:
We can classify the equilibrium solutions of an autonomous ODE ${y}^{′}=f(y)$ by examining its phase line.

- An equilibrium solution is a *sink* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

- We're given that $y=-4$ and $y=-1$ are equilibrium points. We represent this on the phase line by drawing two distinct points at these locations.

- We're given that $y=-1$ is a source. We represent this on the phase line by drawing an upward-pointing arrow just above $y=-1$ and a downward-pointing arrow just below it.

- We're given that $y=-4$ is a sink. We represent this on the phase line by drawing a downward-pointing arrow just above $y=-4$ (already drawn by the above property) and an upward-pointing arrow just below it.

Therefore, our phase line is as follows:

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Vector Field Corresponding to a Given Potential Function
question.problem: For which of the following vector fields is $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}yz+{z}^{2}$ a potential function?
question.worked_solution:
A vector field $F$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $F.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}yz+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}yz+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2xyz\,i+{x}^{2}z\,j+({x}^{2}y+2z)\,k \\  & =F\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
F=2xyz\,i+{x}^{2}z\,j+({x}^{2}y+2z)\,k.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Extreme Values of a Constrained Quadratic Function
question.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+5\,$ on the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0.$
question.worked_solution:
We must find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=0
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨8x,4y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}8x=2\lambda x \\ 4y=\lambda (2y-2)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}x(4-\lambda )=0 \\ y(\lambda -2)=\lambda \end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-2y & =0\,⇒\,y=0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,0),(0,2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =4$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4-2)=4\,⇒\,y=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,2).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,0),\,(0,2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(0,2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $5$ | $13$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at the point $(0,2)$ and its maximum value is $13.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}⟨2t-1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{1}^{4}(2t-1)\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨({t}^{2}-t)\,\,{|}_{1}^{4},\,\sqrt{t}\,\,{|}_{1}^{4}\,\,⟩ \\  & =⟨\text{ }({4}^{2}-4)-({1}^{2}-1),\,\sqrt{4}-\sqrt{1}⟩ \\  & =⟨12,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Multiple Parts of the Decomposition
question.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}7-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}7-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

question.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Using the Complex Conjugate
question.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3-2\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=3+2\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1),1,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)⟩, \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1),0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1),1,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1),0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1) & 1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1) \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1) & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1)\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1) \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1)\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1) \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1)\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1) & 1 \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1) & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1)-0,-({sin}^{2}⁡(2t-1)+{cos}^{2}⁡(2t-1)),0+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-1),-1,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Specific Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,-1,\sqrt{3}⟩, \\ N(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,-\sqrt{3},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =T(\frac{\pi }{6})\times N(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,-1,\sqrt{3}⟩\times \frac{1}{2}⟨0,-\sqrt{3},-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & -\sqrt{3} & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & \sqrt{3} \\ -\sqrt{3} & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & -\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨(1+3),-(0-0),(0-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨4,0,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
question.problem: If ${F}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩$ and $F(1)=⟨-1,\,2⟩,$ then $F(t)=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨-1,\,2⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-1,\,2⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-1,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-1,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)⟩.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-0,-(-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}),-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$
